subject: Aggregating data and creating variables on the fly

messages.author: f2b88983b2560339
messages.subject: Aggregating data and creating variables on the fly
parts:
Hi,

I've got a problem that I think should be doable with dplyr, but I'm not able to think straight.

I have a data frame that contains log data from a learning management system with the variables "action", "userid" and "time". And additional variable contains different time frames, e.g. "time >= 0 & time < 1", "time >=1 & time < 3", "time >=3 & time < 6".

Now I want to aggregate these variables for each user, for example the number of logins per user and time frame. Doing this with several filter() could be one solution, but it would be easier if I could simply take the filters from the time frame variable and create the summary variables on the fly, so that I end up with data like this:

userid login1 login2 login3
001      2         3        2
014      1         4        3

Pseudocode idea

filter("action" == "login"){
   for each time frame do{
      for each user do{
         sum(nrow)
      }
   }
}

But I don't want to use loops, so how could the solution look like using dplyr (and lapply,...)? Any suggestions are highly appreciated!

Kind regards

   Bjoern

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Aggregating data and creating variables on the fly
parts:
In the absence of a reproducible example, the following code is pure
speculation, but given your description, it might be a reasonable
place to start.

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Let DF be the name of your data frame with columns userid and time;
# action appears to be just another grouping variable, so you could add it
# to the group_by() statement below.

DF %>% mutate(timeint = cut(time, c(0, 1, 3, 6),
include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
group_by(userid, timeint) %>%
summarise(n = n()) %>%
mutate(timeint = factor(timeint, labels =
paste0("login", 1:3))) %>%
spread(timeint, n)

The first step is to discretize time into subintervals using cut();
the result is a factor. We then group by userid and timeint and
compute the number of observations in each
combination. We then use mutate() again to relabel the levels of
timeint and finally use tidyr::spread() to convert from long to wide
form with respect to login times.

As Hadley mentioned, it's much easier to write code when you have a
concrete example from which to work. Google 'reproducible example R'
to find several excellent posts that describe how to write a
productive reproducible example for any of the R-related mailing lists
(including one from Hadley!).

HTH,
Dennis
